lessons.title: Caching in depth: exact, semantic and embedding caches
points: Why cache an LLM app: latency, cost and the provider's rate-limit budget; measured as hit rate, false-hit rate, latency saved and tokens/$ saved.
Exact-match cache key: a hash of the normalized prompt + model + settings; normalization (case, whitespace, punctuation) raises the hit rate without wrong answers.
Semantic cache lookup: embed the question, find the nearest cached question, and reuse its answer when the similarity is above a threshold.
What a semantic cache entry stores: question text, its embedding, the answer, model, prompt version, index version, sources, tenant/scope, created_at, TTL and hit count.
Choosing the similarity threshold from data: paraphrase pairs (should hit) vs near-miss pairs (must not hit), precision and false hits at each threshold.
Near-miss protection: an entity guard so numbers, IDs, dates and names in the question must match before a cached answer is reused.
Storage backends: in-memory, SQLite, PostgreSQL + pgvector and Redis (vector search) run and compared on lookup latency, persistence, TTL support and operating cost.
Other semantic-cache stores and when to pick them: Valkey, MongoDB Atlas, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Cassandra and managed cache services.
What to cache: FAQ-style answers, retrieval results, embeddings (CacheBackedEmbeddings), reranker scores and slow tool results.
What never to cache: personalised or permission-dependent answers, time-sensitive data, actions with side effects, errors, refusals and low-confidence answers.
Invalidation: TTLs, version keys (model, prompt version, index version) so re-ingesting changed documents retires stale answers, and explicit purge on source change.
Scoping and safety: separate caches per tenant, user group, language and access rights; personal data in cache entries; cache poisoning.
Provider prompt caching (repeated prompt prefixes billed cheaper) vs response caching: different mechanisms, often used together.
Caching in production: cache-stampede protection (request coalescing), warm-up with the top questions, size limits and eviction, and hit-rate metrics on a dashboard.

lessons.title: Retrieval metrics in depth: hit, precision, recall, nDCG, MAP, F1 and MRR
points: hit@k (hit rate, success@k): did at least one relevant chunk reach the top k? The "can the model answer at all" rate.
MRR: the mean of 1/rank of the first relevant chunk; rewards putting the answer first.
precision@k: the share of the k returned chunks that are relevant; the rest is noise that costs tokens and can mislead the model.
recall@k: the share of ALL relevant chunks in the index that were returned; it matters when an answer is spread over several chunks.
Counting every relevant chunk in the index: evidence-based labels make the denominator of recall and nDCG computable without hand labelling.
Answerability: the share of questions where some indexed chunk contains the whole answer; chunking can split an answer so no chunk holds it, even when the file is indexed.
nDCG@k: relevant chunks score more the higher they rank, divided by the score of the ideal ranking; the standard metric for comparing rankers and rerankers.
MAP@k: precision measured at each relevant rank, averaged per question and then over questions.
F1@k: the harmonic mean of precision@k and recall@k, one number for the precision/recall balance.
The k trade-off: as k grows, hit rate and recall rise while precision falls and context tokens grow; choose k from the curve and the token budget.
Report several cutoffs (@1, @3, @5), slices by question type and source, and average per question so every question counts equally.

Which metric for which decision: hit rate and recall for loading, chunking and first-stage retrieval; precision, nDCG and MRR for reranking and choosing k; coverage and answerability for loaders and OCR.
